title: DNS Records and Tools
about: Read the answers a name lookup gives back, and spot lookalike names.

cards.title: One name, many answers
cards.body:
DNS keeps each kind of answer in its own **record**:

- **A**: the website's [[IPv4]] address (an **AAAA** record holds its [[IPv6]] address).
- **CNAME**: an alias, meaning "look up this other name instead".
- **MX**: where the domain's **email** goes.

When you look something up, you ask for one kind of record.

cards.prompt:
Your club's `example.org` needs a website address and somewhere for email.

Does [[DNS]] give one answer per name, or several?

options.text: Several: one name holds answers for different jobs
One: each name has one IP address for everything
options.nudge: Your first lookup already gave example.com two addresses.

options.text: One: email doesn't use DNS, only the website does
options.nudge: Email must find its server too, and finding servers by name is DNS's job.

options.text: One: email needs a separate domain of its own
options.nudge: Club email can use the same name, `hello@example.org`: could one name hold more answers?

cards.explanation: One name can hold **several** answers: your first `nslookup` showed two addresses, and a domain can also say where email goes. The website and mail server are often different machines.
cards.hint: How many addresses came back from your first `nslookup`?

cards.prompt: Each record holds one kind of answer for example.com. Match each record to a value it could hold.
cards.explanation: **A** holds an IPv4 address (dots) and **AAAA** an IPv6 one (colons). **CNAME** holds another *name* (`www` is an alias for `example.com`), and **MX** names the mail [[server]].
cards.hint: Dots, colons or a name? Of the two names, which sounds like a place for email?
cards.nudge: Dots mean [[IPv4]] and colons [[IPv6]]; of the names, one is the main domain and one a mail server.

cards.prompt: The club site `example.org` loads fine. Which extra record lets mail to `hello@example.org` arrive?

options.text: An MX record naming the club's mail server
A second A record with the website's address again
options.nudge: The site already works: email needs a record that says where *mail* goes.

options.text: An AAAA record with an IPv6 address for the site
options.nudge: AAAA gives the site another kind of address: email needs a record naming the mail server.

options.text: A CNAME record pointing example.org to another name
options.nudge: A CNAME only says "look up this other name instead": which record is about email?

cards.explanation: An **MX** record tells other mail servers where to deliver example.org's email. A and AAAA give the site's addresses, and a CNAME points to another name.
cards.hint: Look back at the list: which record is about mail?

cards.prompt: Run `dig www.example.com`. This time the answer has two lines.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal, with dig's output shortened to just the answer. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Look up www.example.com and show the answer
commands.output:
;; ANSWER SECTION:
www.example.com.	1800	IN	CNAME	example.com.
example.com.		1800	IN	A	198.51.100.10

success.question: www.example.com is an alias for which name?

cards.explanation: Line 1 is a **CNAME**: `www.example.com` is an alias for `example.com`. The [[resolver]] followed it to example.com's **A** record, `198.51.100.10`.
cards.hint: Look at the line with `CNAME` in it: the name at its end is what it points to.
cards.nudge: Use the `CNAME` line, not the `A` line: the target is a name, not an address.

cards.prompt: Put the steps in order for a [[browser]] opening `www.example.com`.

items.label: Get a CNAME: an alias for example.com
Look up the A record for example.com

cards.explanation: A CNAME holds a name, not an address, so the lookup carries on with **example.com** to its **A** record. Only then can the browser connect.
cards.hint: A CNAME holds a name, and you can't connect without a real address.
cards.nudge: Each lookup comes before its answer: what does the alias make the lookup do next?

cards.prompt: A message says "Log in to your example.com account". Which link really belongs to **example.com**?

options.nudge: Check every character: one of them isn't the letter it seems.
It starts with the right words, but what does it end with? The right-hand end decides.
A hyphen makes a new name, and this one ends in a different domain.

cards.explanation: `login.example.com` ends in **example.com**, so its owner controls it. `examp1e.com` uses a **1** for an **l**, and the other two end in **example.org**: scammers rely on lookalikes, so always check the right-hand end.
cards.hint: Check the right-hand end of each name, letter by letter.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- One name can hold several **records**, one for each job.
- **A** gives an address, **CNAME** an alias, **MX** the mail server.
- `nslookup` and `dig` let you ask [[DNS]] questions yourself.
